entities.name: Guillaume de Harsigny
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Guillaume de Harsigny (died July 10, 1393) emerged as a preeminent French physician in the late 14th century, whose career significantly illuminated the evolving role of medical practitioners within European royal courts. Serving as a trusted court physician to King Charles V of France (reigned 1364–1380), and subsequently to his son Charles VI, Harsigny was at the nexus of political power and medical science during a period marked by recurrent plagues, warfare, and growing medical professionalism. His reputation for keen observation and practical treatment placed him among the most respected medical authorities of his generation, influencing both royal health policy and the broader perception of the physician's craft in the Medieval era.

His most notable professional engagement involved the meticulous care of King Charles V, who suffered from chronic gout and other debilitating conditions. Harsigny's treatment strategies, though grounded in the humoral theory prevalent at the time, also emphasized diet, regimen, and empirical observation, a pragmatic approach that likely contributed to Charles V's relatively stable health despite his ailments. Following Charles V's death, Harsigny continued his service to the Valois dynasty, accompanying King Charles VI on military campaigns, such as the expedition to Ghent in 1382, demonstrating the physician's expanded role beyond the sickroom to include advisory and even logistical capacities within the royal retinue. His daily proximity to the monarch provided him with unparalleled insight into the intersection of royal health and statecraft.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guillaume de Harsigny's role as a trusted court physician to two French kings significantly elevated the status of medical professionals in royal courts. His pragmatic approach to medicine and his direct influence on powerful monarchs contributed to the professionalization of the medical field in Europe.
